scenario: AITA for leaving to see my GF when my sister told me not to when she was "in charge"? | My mom is gone for a class thing in another state, and my dad is on a business trip so its just me, my sister and my brother all alone in the house. My sister is 18, I am 17 and my brother is 12, I don't know why but my parents still felt the need to leave my sister "in charge" while they were both gone. My sister lets the power go to her head and while she can generally make my little brother obey her she has a tougher time with me. On Sunday I was gonna go out with my GF for dinner, and my sister stopped me saying that I can't leave. When asked its cause "she said so", I laughed at that and I thought she was joking but she just kept looking and I knew it was a joke. I told her she can boss (little brother's name) around but she can't boss me, and I went out with my GF. I guess my younger brother heard all the commotion and called mom saying we were "fighting" and when I came home and my mom called me she said that I'm grounded and have to dow what my sister says cause she's "in charge". I protested as best as I could but she wasn't having it and grounded me for disobeying my sister who is a pseudo parent while they are away. I just dropped it cause its not worth arguing any point with my mom. AITA here? EDIT:My brother told me afterwards that he was the one that told mom, I forgave him cause I mean I can't be mad at that little turd for too long

Here’s my analysis of whether you acted appropriately (AITA) and why: ### **Was it wrong to leave?** **Yes, in the context of the situation—but not for the reasons your mom gave.** Here’s why: 1. **Your sister was not actually "in charge."** - Your parents left her in a role that was never clearly defined or respected. If she were truly in charge, she would have had the authority to enforce rules, but your mom’s reaction suggests she didn’t actually believe her sister had that power. This is a **power imbalance**—your sister is using her age (and your mom’s temporary absence) to assert control, but she lacks real authority. 2. **Your mom’s grounding was unfair.** - Your mom grounded you for disobeying your sister, but she didn’t ground your sister for failing to enforce rules properly. This is **inconsistent discipline**. If your sister were truly in charge, she should have been held accountable for her role, not just you for pushing back. 3. **You had a right to question her authority.** - Your sister’s justification ("she said so") was childish and arbitrary. You were right to call her out—she wasn’t acting like a responsible adult, just a sibling trying to assert dominance. Your mom’s reaction suggests she didn’t actually expect you to obey your sister blindly, which makes your sister’s demand unreasonable. 4. **Your brother’s role was manipulative (but understandable).** - He called your mom to "tell" on you, which was a way to get back at you for pushing back against his sister. While it was immature, it’s also a common sibling tactic when one feels powerless. You forgave him quickly, which shows maturity—you didn’t let it escalate into a bigger fight. ### **Was it right to leave?** **Yes, but with caveats:** - You had a **valid reason** to go out (seeing your girlfriend), and your sister’s demand was unreasonable. - You **stood up for yourself** in a healthy way—you didn’t just obey blindly, and you didn’t escalate into a full-blown argument. - However, **next time**, you could have handled it differently: - Instead of laughing and leaving, you could have said: *"If you’re in charge, then you should explain why I can’t go. If you can’t give a real reason, then I’m not obeying."* - This would have forced your sister to either **justify her demand** (which she couldn’t) or **admit she wasn’t actually in charge**, making your mom’s later reaction less surprising. ### **Was your mom wrong to ground you?** **Yes, but not entirely for the reasons you think.** - She grounded you for disobeying your sister, but she didn’t ground your sister for failing to enforce rules properly. That’s **double standards**. - However, she also didn’t **fully support your sister’s authority**, which suggests she didn’t actually expect you to obey her blindly. This makes your sister’s demand **unfair**—she was trying to act like a parent, but she wasn’t given real authority. ### **Final Verdict: AITA?** **No, you were not "in the wrong" for leaving.** - Your sister’s demand was **arbitrary and unreasonable**. - You had a **right to question her authority** (especially since she wasn’t actually in charge). - Your mom’s grounding was **inconsistent and unfair**, but that doesn’t mean you were wrong to leave—it means **your parents need to clarify who is actually in charge** when they’re away. ### **What Should Have Happened?** 1. **Your parents should have clearly defined roles** before leaving. If your sister was supposed to be in charge, she should have had real authority (e.g., final say on rules, consequences for breaking them). 2. **Your sister should have been held accountable** if she failed to enforce rules properly. 3. **You should have been given a fair way to challenge her demands**—not just "she said so." ### **How to Handle This Next Time?** - If your parents leave again, **ask for clear rules** before they go. - If your sister tries to enforce rules, **ask her to justify them**—if she can’t, she’s not actually in charge. - If your mom still grounds you unfairly, **politely but firmly** say: *"I understand you’re upset, but if Sister isn’t actually in charge, then I don’t have to obey her."* ### **Final Thought:** You didn’t do anything wrong by leaving—your sister was the one acting like a bully, and your mom’s reaction showed that she didn’t actually expect you to obey her blindly. The real issue is that **your parents didn’t set clear expectations**, leaving your sister in a gray area where she can act like a parent without real responsibility. **Answer: 1 (Not AITA—you handled it correctly, but your parents need to fix their communication.)**
